feed.title: What changed on Common Shade
feed.subtitle: Each reviewed change to the free evidence base on extreme heat in South and Southeast Asia

entry.title: The heat network can be narrowed by place, action and part played
entry.summary: A reader can now ask who works on one action in one place, and each listing says what kind of body it is, where its listed work is and whether its link answered a check. Where nothing is listed for a place, the page says not found yet.

entry.title: Listings in the heat network now open on the heat work itself
entry.summary: A first set of listings that linked only to an organisation’s homepage now link to the page that shows its heat work, such as a warning service, a plan or a report. Each new link was opened and read by a check before it replaced the old one.

entry.title: COP31, first check-in: health, early warning and money
entry.summary: In COP31's first days, heat surfaced through a voluntary health initiative, the presidency's health theme, IFRC's finding on early warning and UNEP's adaptation finance gap, rather than through negotiating text. Each was verified at its primary source before joining the COP31 watch, and the watch now says plainly what it has not found yet.

entry.title: A line for AI agents under the homepage's opening
entry.summary: Assistants that read the homepage for someone now meet a short, quiet pointer to the page written for them near the top, as well as in the footer, so the guidance on citing sources and passing on evidence labels is easier to find.

entry.title: How AI is used on Common Shade, stated plainly
entry.summary: Readers deserve to know how a site that asks them to trust its sources is made. The approach page now says what AI does in building Common Shade, what it is never allowed to do, who approves what is published, and where its limits are.

entry.title: Evidence packs to use with your own AI
entry.summary: Many readers already think with an AI assistant or notebook tool, and the site itself runs none. Each country, vicious cycle and action is now one plain-text pack of the site's own words and sources, with questions to start from and a plain warning that the sources, not the assistant, are the authority.

entry.title: A Heat Tool Finder: which tool fits the decision in front of you
entry.summary: People who plan, deliver or fund heat protection often know a decision but not the tool for it. The finder sets warning services, assessments, datasets, modelling tools and guidance side by side, with what each needs, what it gives and what it cannot tell you, and three illustrative workflows that combine them.

entry.title: Open files for the tools that read the web, and a privacy page
entry.summary: Assistants and crawlers look for a site's files at standard addresses. Common Shade now publishes an agent directory, an OpenAPI description of its open data with examples, a change feed and a Markdown twin of every page, and says plainly on one page what it keeps and what it asks other services for.

entry.title: Pages arrive a little sooner, and long lists open faster
entry.summary: A page of the site now starts loading the moment a reader presses on a link to it, and the longest lists lay out only the cards near the screen. On a slowed phone the solutions list opened in about 830 ms instead of 1,120 ms.

entry.title: A page for the AI agents that read the site
entry.summary: More people now meet the site through an assistant than through a browser. /for-ai/ tells an assistant what Common Shade is, when it fits a person's question, how to cite it and what to avoid, and publishes the same record as JSON and plain text, so an assistant can represent the evidence as carefully as the site states it.

entry.title: Are heat plans budgeted, or only hoped for?
entry.summary: After Bangkok's strategy found money to build but not always to run, a reading of heat plans from India and Bangladesh showed a nearby pattern: costs and potential funders are named, but budgets that recur each season rarely are. Each claim was written from passages checked on GitHub.

entry.title: A planning question for heatwaves longer than any on record
entry.summary: Plans and budgets are usually sized to the worst heatwave people remember, and new modelling suggests some future heatwaves will run longer. The workbook now asks whether the money and staff would last.

entry.title: Signals: which way heat policy is moving
entry.summary: Announcements are the earliest sign of where heat policy is heading, but on their own they are weak evidence. Signals places each one on a ladder from announced to evaluated, starting with COP31 and this year's signals already on the site, so readers can weigh them rather than collect them.

entry.title: COP31 opens: the climate behind this year's heat
entry.summary: As COP31 opened, WMO reported that 2026 will be one of the four warmest years on record and that El Niño is set to bring more heat into 2027, while UNEP's Emissions Gap Report found that warming will overshoot 1.5 °C. Each was verified at its primary source before joining the COP31 watch on Signals.

entry.title: What Bangkok's heat plan costs, and what stands between plans and money
entry.summary: Bangkok's 2026 financing strategy, from UNDP and the city, costs the city's heat plan and explains why running costs, not ambition, are the gap. Each insight was tied to the strategy's own words and checked on GitHub before it reached the site, and the city page now credits the heat plan to the city itself.

entry.title: How heat became visible: a graded timeline of when the world began to notice
entry.summary: Knowing when science, health, labour, finance and the UN each noticed heat shows who was still missing. Each event carries a grade, so certainty is never overstated.

entry.title: Correction: what cooling centres and fans can and cannot do
entry.summary: Readers plan real protection from these pages. Saying what the evidence supports, and what it depends on, keeps a plan from resting on more than the evidence holds.

entry.title: Lenses on what the map was missing
entry.summary: The map now separates more of the people it had grouped together, adds slow and hidden harms and compound events, and shows where places differ. Each addition passed a number-by-number audit against its source.

entry.title: Watch for: documented side effects of actions that otherwise help
entry.summary: An action can help one group and burden another. Showing documented side effects next to each action is a revised reading of what helps, not a reason to stop.

entry.title: Who could help a household through a hot season, country by country
entry.summary: Public schemes could cushion lost work and care costs in a hot season. Setting out who runs each, what it gives and how far people get through the steps of access shows where support stops.

entry.title: The news page now shows what became of each paper and headline
entry.summary: Coverage and checked evidence are easy to confuse. Every paper on the news page now goes through the weekly evidence review, and each item shows whether it is on the Evidence map, in review, set aside or still waiting.

entry.title: Every open question now carries its own dated history
entry.summary: A question that moves is easier to trust than one that simply changes. Each step now shows when it happened, what moved it and which records did, and advanced is never shown as answered.

entry.title: Questions opened for every step of access nobody has measured
entry.summary: Many steps between a scheme on paper and support in hand are unmeasured, especially whether support is adequate and on time. Each gap now carries a question and a study that could answer it.

entry.title: How Singapore organises for heat, traced to its own sources
entry.summary: A country brief from the Southeast Asia heat-health hub described the coordination, triggers and research money behind Singapore's heat rules. Each insight was traced to the government or published source behind it, and only what those sources confirm reached the site.

entry.title: A rule on paper is no longer read as a result
entry.summary: The method grouped official records with measured findings as known. An official record can show that a rule or scheme exists; whether it was carried out or worked takes an evaluation, and the method now says so.

entry.title: Every harm paired with hope: the nearest places to act, or an honest gap
entry.summary: A harm without a way forward can leave a reader stuck. Each harm now points to the actions closest to it, or says plainly that none is documented yet.

entry.title: India's Heat Resilient Cities Framework (2026), across the site
entry.summary: The framework moves cities from emergency response towards lasting change, with the people most exposed at the centre. It now informs the glossary, the planning checklist and the cities it names.

entry.title: India heat action plan archive: verified plans and guidance from across India
entry.summary: Plans are easier to learn from side by side. Each one is verified, typed and dated as printed, so a city can find a neighbour's plan and see how it changed.

entry.title: Heat and the health of mothers, children and minds
entry.summary: Pregnancy, newborn health, mental health and gender-based violence were thin on the map. Adding them, with an evidence brief, makes these harms visible next to the better-known ones.

entry.title: A weekly evidence review, signed off by a person
entry.summary: New studies arrive every week. A Monday harvest opens a review, and only studies a person accepts join their cycles, so the map grows without lowering its bar.
